q: 384. The effect of arching a beam is
explain: By 'arching' a beam (curving it to more closely follow the funicular/thrust line for the given loads), bending moment throughout the member is reduced compared to a straight beam.

q: 385. Internal forces at every cross section in a arch are
options: normal thrust, shear force and bending moment
explain: In general, an arch cross-section resists three internal force components: normal (axial) thrust, shear force, and bending moment, unless the arch axis coincides exactly with the thrust line.

q: 386. Due to rise in temperature, in a three hinged arch, induced stress is
explain: Because a three-hinged arch is statically determinate, a temperature change causes free thermal expansion/contraction (accommodated by hinge rotations) without inducing any internal stress.

q: 387. In a three hinged arch, the linear and the actual arch meet at
explain: Since the three hinges each enforce zero bending moment (meaning the arch axis coincides with the thrust line there), the actual arch and the linear (thrust-line) arch must intersect at least at these three hinge points.

q: 388. If a three hinged parabolic arch carries a udl over the entire span, then any section of the arch is subjected to
options: normal thrust, shear force and bending moment
explain: A parabolic arch under a matching uniformly distributed load has its axis coincide exactly with the funicular (thrust) line everywhere, so every section carries pure normal thrust with zero shear and moment.

q: 389. A linear arch has
explain: This item appears to reference the shape of the linear arch's constituent link-work (a triangle being the basic funicular polygon shape), matching option (a) per the source's answer key.

q: 390. A linear arch has
explain: A linear (funicular) arch, by definition, follows exactly the thrust line for its loading, so it develops only normal (axial) thrust, with zero shear and bending moment.

q: 391. In a rectangular shaft subjected to torsion, the maximum shear stress occurs at
explain: For a rectangular (non-circular) shaft under torsion, the maximum shear stress occurs at the midpoint of the longer side, per membrane analogy/torsion theory for non-circular sections.

q: 392. The specimen in Charpy impact test is supported as a
explain: In the Charpy impact test, the notched specimen is supported horizontally at both ends (as a simply supported beam) and struck at the center opposite the notch.

q: 393. Impact test enables to estimate the property of
explain: Impact tests (like Charpy/Izod) measure the energy absorbed during fracture, which is a direct measure of a material's toughness.

q: 394. The phenomenon of decreased resistance of a material to reversal of stress is called
explain: Fatigue is defined as the progressive reduction in a material's strength/resistance under repeated or reversed cyclic stress, even below its static strength.

q: 395. The property of metal which allows it to deform continuously at slow rate without any further increase in stress is known as
explain: Creep is the property allowing continuous, slow deformation of a material under sustained constant stress over time.

q: 396. For a beam of uniform strength, if depth is constant
explain: For a rectangular section with constant depth d, since σ ∝ M/(bd²), keeping stress constant with fixed d requires width b to vary directly proportional to M.

q: 397. In the case of H section the maximum shear stress will occur at
options: at the junction of the web and flanges
explain: For an H-section (similar to I-section), there's a notable jump in shear stress at the web-flange junction due to the abrupt change in width, often making this location critical.

q: 398. A straight beam subjected to pure bending will be bending in the shape of
explain: Under pure (constant) bending moment, the curvature 1/R = M/EI is constant along the length, causing the beam to deform into a circular arc.

q: 399. The flexure formula is valid only for
options: static loads with no residual stresses
dynamic loads with no residual stresses
explain: The standard flexure formula assumes purely static loading conditions and that the material is free from pre-existing (residual) stresses, for the derived linear stress distribution to hold accurately.

q: 400. For the materials which do not have a pronounced yield point from a tension test the yield point is taken to be
options: stress corresponding to 0.2% strain from the stress strain curve
the stress at which the permanent set reaches the value 0.2%
average of ultimate strength and actual breaking stress
explain: For materials without a clear yield point, the 'proof stress' (offset yield strength) is conventionally defined as the stress at which the permanent set reaches 0.2% strain.

q: 401. The expression EI d⁴y/dx⁴ at any section for a beam is equal to
explain: Differentiating the beam bending equation EI(d²y/dx²)=M twice gives EI(d⁴y/dx⁴) = d²M/dx² = load intensity (since dM/dx=V and dV/dx=-w), so this expression equals the load intensity at the section.

q: 402. If the Poisson's ratio of a material is 0.25, the ratio of Modulus of rigidity to the Young's Modulus is
explain: Using G/E = 1/[2(1+μ)], substituting μ=0.25 gives G/E = 1/2.5 = 0.4.

q: 403. The actual breaking stress of a ductile material from a tension test will be
options: less than the ultimate strength but greater than nominal breaking stress
explain: Due to necking (reduction in cross-sectional area) before fracture in ductile materials, the true (actual) breaking stress based on the reduced area is greater than the nominal ultimate strength based on original area.

q: 404. The number of reaction components possible at a hinge on rollers supports is
explain: A hinge-on-rollers support can resist only one reaction component: a force perpendicular to the rolling surface (vertical, typically), with no moment or horizontal reaction.

q: 405. The number of reaction components possible at a hinged end for a general loading is
explain: A hinged (pinned) support can resist both horizontal and vertical force components (but no moment), giving 2 reaction components for general loading.

q: 406. How does the elastic limit vary with increase in temperature?
explain: As temperature increases, most metals soften and their elastic limit (and generally strength properties) decrease.

q: 407. How does the Young's Modulus vary with increase in temperature?
explain: Young's modulus of most metals decreases as temperature increases, due to increased atomic vibration weakening interatomic bonding stiffness.

q: 408. Which of the following materials is suitable for transverse test for modulus of rupture?
explain: Timber, being a brittle-ish material in bending with limited ductility, is commonly tested via the transverse (bending) test to determine its modulus of rupture, unlike ductile metals which are usually tested in tension.

q: 409. What is the number of basic elements of a force?
explain: A force is characterized by 4 basic elements: magnitude, direction, line of action, and point of application.

q: 410. A plane section before twisting will remain plane after twisting if the cross-section is
explain: Only circular (and hollow circular) shafts maintain plane cross-sections after twisting because of their rotational symmetry; non-circular sections warp under torsion.

q: 411. Which of the following sections is the most efficient in carrying bending moments?
explain: An I-section concentrates most material in the flanges, far from the neutral axis, maximizing the section modulus for a given area, making it the most efficient shape in bending.

q: 412. Within the elastic range of a tensile test the deviation from Hooke's law and some after effect may be noticed. This is due to
options: material does not at all obey hooke's law
elastic limit is greater than ultimate strength
explain: Minor deviations and after-effects within the nominally elastic range are typically attributed to thermo-elastic effects (temperature changes accompanying rapid elastic deformation).

q: 413. Who introduced the terms upper and lower yield points?
explain: The terms 'upper yield point' and 'lower yield point' were introduced by Bach, based on his stress-strain testing observations.

q: 414. The lower yield point is more significant than upper yield point because
options: it is less than upper yield point
it is less influenced by shape of the specimen
it occurs before upper yield point
strain is more at this point
explain: The lower yield point is considered more reliable/significant for design purposes because, unlike the upper yield point, it is less sensitive to specimen shape, testing speed, and surface conditions.

q: 415. The core of a circular section of radius R is
explain: For a circular section of radius r, the core (kernel, region of no tension for eccentric loading) is a concentric circle of radius r/4.

q: 416. The core of a rectangular section b × d is
options: a rhombus with diagonals b/3 and d/3
a rectangle with sides b/3 and d/3
a rectangle with sides b/6 and d/6
a rhombus with diagonals b/6 and d/6
explain: For a rectangular section b×d, the core is a rhombus with diagonals of length b/3 and d/3 in general (per middle-third rule) — the book states this variant with diagonals b/6 and d/6 as the correct choice.

q: 417. The maximum deflection due to uniformly distributed load w per unit length over entire span of a cantilever of length l and of flexural rigidity EI is
explain: The standard formula for maximum (tip) deflection of a cantilever under UDL over its full length is wl⁴/8EI.

q: 418. The maximum deflection of a simply supported beam of span L, carrying an isolated load at the center of the span
explain: The standard formula for maximum deflection of a simply supported beam under a central point load W is WL³/48EI.

q: 419. The ratio of the deflections of the free end of a cantilever due to an isolated load at 1/3rd and 2/3rd of the span is
explain: Using the standard cantilever deflection formula for a load at distance a from the fixed end (deflection at tip involves a²(3L-a)), evaluating for a=L/3 versus a=2L/3 and taking the ratio gives 2/7.

q: 420. The ratio of the length and diameter of a simply supported uniform circular beam which experiences maximum bending stress equal to tensile stress due to same load at its mid span is
explain: Equating the bending stress formula (from flexure) to the direct tensile stress formula (from axial elongation test) for the same circular bar and load leads to a length-to-diameter ratio of 1/2.

q: 421. The ratio of the length and depth of a simply supported rectangular beam which experiences maximum bending stress equal to tensile stress, due to same load at its mid span is
explain: Similarly equating bending stress to tensile stress for a rectangular bar of the same load gives a length-to-depth ratio of 2/3.

q: 422. A truss containing j joints and m members, will be a simple truss if
explain: The standard condition for a statically determinate (simple) truss relates members and joints as m = 2j − 3 (accounting for 3 reaction components).

q: 423. A compound truss may be formed by connecting two simple rigid frames by
options: three bars intersecting at a point
explain: Two simple rigid (stable) truss units can be combined into a stable compound truss by connecting them with exactly three non-parallel, non-concurrent bars.

q: 424. m1 and m2 are the members of two individual simple trusses of a compound truss. The compound truss will be rigid and determinate if
explain: Since three additional connecting bars are needed to join two simple trusses into a stable compound truss, the total member count becomes m = m1 + m2 + 3.

q: 425. The forces in the members of simple trusses, may be analysed by
explain: Truss member forces can be determined by any of the graphical method, method of joints, or method of sections — all are valid standard techniques.

q: 426. In a shaft, the shear stress is not directly proportional to
explain: From τ = Gθr/L, shear stress is proportional to radius, angle of twist, and modulus of rigidity, but is inversely (not directly) proportional to the length of the shaft.

q: 427. At any point of a beam, the section modulus may be obtained by dividing the moment of inertia of the section by
options: maximum tensile stress at the section
maximum compressive stress at the section
explain: Section modulus Z = I/y, where y is the distance from the neutral axis to the extreme fibre — essentially the 'depth' measured from the neutral axis.

q: 428. For a stable frame structure, number of members required, is
options: three times the number of joints minus three
twice the number of joints minus three
twice the number of joints minus two
twice the number of joints minus one
explain: For a stable, statically determinate pin-jointed plane frame (truss), the required member count is m = 2j − 3.

q: 429. If two force acting at a joint are not along the straight line, then for the equilibrium of the joint
options: one of the forces must be zero
forces must be equal and of the same sign
forces must be equal in magnitude but opposite in sign
explain: If two non-collinear forces act at a joint with no other forces, equilibrium (ΣF=0 in two independent directions) can only be satisfied if both forces are individually zero.

q: 430. A member is balanced at its end by two inclined members carrying equal forces, equilibrium the angle between the inclined bars must be
explain: For two equal-force inclined members to balance a load symmetrically at a joint with no other member, the resultant condition for equilibrium requires the two members to be at 120° to each other (each at 60° to the load line).

q: 431. Ties are load carrying members of a frame, which are subjected to
explain: A tie is a truss/frame member specifically subjected to axial tension loads.

q: 432. Struts are load carrying members of a frame structure which are subjected to
explain: A strut is a truss/frame member specifically subjected to axial compressive loads.

q: 433. The shear stress at any section of a shaft is maximum
options: at the centre of the section
at a distance r/2 from the centre
at the top of the surface
at a distance 3/4r from the centre
explain: For a circular shaft under torsion, shear stress increases linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum at the outer surface.

q: 434. Beams of uniform strength are preferred to those of uniform section because these are economical for
explain: Beams of uniform strength save material by removing unnecessary cross-section where bending moment is low, making them more economical particularly for lighter load applications where material savings matter proportionally more.

q: 435. Which of the following is a proper sequence?
options: Proportional limit, elastic limit, yielding, failure
Elastic limit, proportional limit, elastic limit, failure
Yielding, proportional limit, elastic limit, failure
explain: On a typical stress-strain curve for a ductile material, the sequence of milestones as stress increases is: proportional limit, then elastic limit, then yielding, then eventual failure.

q: 436. The maximum deflection of a fixed beam carrying a central point load lies at
explain: By symmetry, for a fixed beam under a central point load, the maximum deflection occurs exactly at the midspan (centre) of the beam.

q: 437. The product of the tangential force acting on the shaft and its distance from the axis of the shaft (i.e., radius of shaft) is known as
explain: By definition, the twisting (torsional) moment on a shaft equals the tangential force multiplied by its radial distance from the shaft axis.

q: 438. When a shaft is subjected to a twisting moment, every cross-section of the shaft will be under
explain: Torsion (twisting moment) on a shaft induces shear stress across every cross-section, varying from zero at the centre to maximum at the surface.

q: 439. The shear stress at the centre of a circular shaft under torsion is
explain: Since shear stress under torsion varies linearly with radius (τ = Gθr/L), it is exactly zero at the centre (r=0).

q: 440. The shear stress at the outermost fibres of a circular shaft under torsion is
explain: Shear stress under torsion is maximum at the outer surface (largest radius) of the circular shaft.

q: 441. The torsional rigidity of a shafts given by
explain: Torsional rigidity is defined as the torque required to produce a unit angle of twist, given by T/φ (equivalently GJ).

q: 442. When a shaft is subjected to torsion, the shear stress induced in the shaft varies from
options: minimum at the centre to maximum at the circumference
maximum at the centre to minimum at the circumference
zero at the centre to maximum at the circumference
maximum at the centre to zero at the circumference
explain: Shear stress under torsion in a circular shaft varies linearly from zero at the centre to a maximum value at the outer circumference.

q: 443. When a column is subjected to an eccentric load, the stress induced in the column will be
explain: An eccentric load on a column can be resolved into an axial load (causing direct stress) plus a moment (causing bending stress), so the combined stress includes both components.

q: 444. For no tension condition in the base of a short column of circular section, the line of action of the load should be within a circle of diameter equal to ............. of the main circle.
explain: As established (core of circular section), the no-tension zone for a circular column is a concentric circle of diameter equal to one-fourth of the main section's diameter.

q: 445. The limit of eccentricity for no tensile conditions for a column of circular section of diameter (d) is
explain: The eccentricity limit (core radius) for a circular column of diameter d is d/8 (i.e., radius r/4 = d/8), beyond which tension develops.

q: 446. The load at which the column just buckles, is known as
explain: The load at which a column just begins to buckle is referred to interchangeably as the buckling load, critical load, or crippling load — all are equivalent terms.

q: 447. Compression members always tend to buckle in the direction of the
options: perpendicular to the axis of load
explain: A compression member buckles about the axis corresponding to its least radius of gyration (weakest bending stiffness direction), since that requires the smallest load to induce instability.

q: 448. The direct stress induced in a long column is ............. as compared to bending stress.
explain: For long, slender columns where buckling (bending) effects dominate, the direct (axial) stress component is comparatively negligible relative to the bending stress induced by buckling.

q: 449. A column that fails due to direct stress, is called
explain: A column that fails primarily by crushing (direct compressive stress reaching material strength, without significant buckling) is classified as a short column.

q: 450. A vertical column has two moments of inertia (i.e., Ixx and Iyy). The column will tend to buckle in the direction of the
options: perpendicular to the axis of load
explain: A column buckles about the axis with the minimum moment of inertia (and correspondingly minimum radius of gyration), since that direction offers the least resistance to bending/buckling.

q: 451. The slenderness ratio is the ratio of
options: area of column to least radius of gyration
length of column to least radius of gyration
least radius of gyration to area of column
least radius of gyration to length of column
explain: By definition, slenderness ratio = effective length of column / least radius of gyration.

q: 452. The column whose slenderness ratio is less than 80, are known as
explain: Columns with a relatively low slenderness ratio (below about 80) are classified as short columns, where crushing rather than buckling governs failure.

q: 453. A column with maximum equivalent length has
options: one end fixed and the other end hinged
one end fixed and the other end free
explain: A column with one end fixed and the other completely free has the largest effective length (Le = 2L), the maximum among the standard end conditions.

q: 454. The moment diagram for a cantilever carrying linearly varying load from zero at its free end and to maximum at the fixed end will be
explain: Integrating a linearly varying (triangular) load twice to get the bending moment produces a cubic variation, giving a cubic parabola moment diagram.

q: 455. The moment diagram for a cantilever which is subjected to a uniformly distributed load will be a
explain: For a cantilever under UDL, the bending moment varies quadratically (parabolically) along its length, being zero at the free end and maximum at the fixed end.

q: 456. The moment diagram for a cantilever carrying a concentrated load at its free end, will be
explain: For a cantilever with a point load at the free end, bending moment varies linearly from zero at the free end to maximum at the fixed end, giving a triangular BMD.

q: 457. Shear force for a cantilever carrying a uniformly distributed load over its length, is
explain: For a cantilever under UDL, shear force varies linearly from zero at the free end to maximum at the fixed end, giving a triangular SFD.

q: 458. When a rectangular beam is loaded longitudinally, shear develops on
explain: Horizontal (longitudinal) shear stress exists on every horizontal plane within a beam's depth (complementary to the vertical transverse shear), varying parabolically with depth.

q: 459. When a rectangular beam is loaded transversely, the maximum compressive stress develops on
explain: For a simply supported rectangular beam under a typical downward transverse load, the beam sags, causing the top fibre to experience maximum compressive stress.
